doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

chapter: The Philly Sound and its makers
title: Motown versus the Philly Sound and Thom Bell's background
summary: Philly sound as sophisticated and jazzier than Motown; Thom Bell's Bacharach influence, Uptown rhythm section and Combs College training.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Yeah and they wouldn't even have to play it again, we'll just like move it over there. When you were working with Gamble and Huff and Thom Bell, I'm trying to frame this idea. Before someone coined the term the Philly Sound, was there a speculation or conversations about what is Motown not doing that we could do? How can we find a niche in the market?

You know I think the big difference between Motown and Philly Sound was Motown was the sound of the young America. It was really a youth movement. R&B. Whereas the Philly sound was a sophisticated, much jazzier much more adult kind of a sound. I mean I've always thought that MFSB could have been the Lionel Hampton band. You know? And in turn, in a way, I was right. MFSB could have gone and played behind Frank Sinatra or anybody. You know? I mean it was that adept at a lot of different styles and adult styles. And I also think that, I also think Gamble, Huff and Bell, they grew up I © Fillius Jazz Archive 9

mean I think Tommy Bell was enamored with Burt Bacharach. And Burt Bacharach was very sophisticated you know? And I think a lot of Thom's arrangements back in those days were like Bacharach arrangements. They would feature a horn player or feature a flute or feature — I mean feature a harp. I mean he had his way of introducing symphonic instruments. And in the '70s, early '70s, that was a big deal I think.
Who was he writing for previous to this? Do you know?

I think that he was — I think that the main rhythm section of the Philly Sound used to work at a place called The Uptown, which was the place where all the Motown groups and all the southern groups would come in and they were the rhythm section. So they were a back—up rhythm section and I think Thom was — played piano in a whole bunch of different kinds of groups. I think as an early 20—year—old, but I think he started having hits pretty soon after that.
Do you know if he was a quote schooled musician?

He definitely went to — he went to some education yes. He had some musical education. There was a place in Philadelphia called the Combs College of Music, that was up in one of the urban neighborhoods in Philadelphia. And I think he took classes there. You know this is before, now every college has courses. You know that. I mean I have nothing to do with any universities at all but every college teaches engineering and teaches music and — in those days that wasn't the case.
